entry.title: Who Holds the Proof? Renters, Documentation, and Administrative Burden in Disaster Assistance

link.title: Who Holds the Proof? Renters, Documentation, and Administrative Burden in Disaster Assistance

entry.content:
Daein Kang and Brian An · Georgia Institute of Technology · Presented at APPAM 2026

When a disaster damages a home, federal assistance often depends on proving that you lived there. But what happens when the records are missing, destroyed, or held by someone else? Homeowners may be able to rely on property records, while renters may need a lease, rent receipt, or statement from a landlord who is also dealing with the disaster.

In “Who Holds the Proof? Housing Tenure, Documentation, and Administrative Burden in Federal Disaster Assistance,” we analyze 22.1 million FEMA Individuals and Households Program applications (2002–2025) to understand whether renters and homeowners face different obstacles when documenting their claims.

We construct a study examining three outcomes in FEMA disaster assistance: application approval, awards amount among approved applicants, and recorded reasons for denial. Using FEMA’s denial classifications, we distinguish documentation-related denials (additional documents required) from substantive denials (ineligible damages or needs, or existing insurance) to identify where disparities between renters and homeowners emerge. We also examine how household income, proximity to Disaster Recovery Centers, and prior local disaster experience are associated with these outcomes. We control for ACS socioeconomic indicators at the ZCTA-level.

Main findings

  • Renters face a distinct documentation barrier. In adjusted models, documentation-related denial is 2.42 percentage points higher for renters (an implied 4.74% versus 2.32% for homeowners), even as renters are 16.09 points less likely to be denied on substantive grounds.
  • The gap persists over time. The renter–homeowner documentation gap is positive every year from 2015 through 2023, reaching 9.97 points in 2020 before narrowing in 2021–2023. The narrowing coincides with expanded FEMA verification options, whether the reforms have caused the change requires further investigation.
  • Income does not resolve the problem. Documentation denials do not steadily decrease with household income. The clearest advantages appear only in the highest income brackets; part of the apparent income gradient reflects differences in tenure.
  • Proximity to Disaster Recovery Centers and recent county disaster experience are also associated with higher approval, though those relationships vary by year.

We find that administrative burden is not only about applicants’ resources; it is also about who controls the evidence an agency requires. When compliance depends on records held by third parties, even well-resourced applicants may face barriers beyond their control. Designing verification procedures that reduce reliance on third-party cooperation, including accepting alternative forms of evidence and enabling agencies to obtain records directly, would alleviate pressure on renters, a group that is already socially vulnerable before, during, and after disasters.

Presented at APPAM 2026 Fall Research Conference. Open or download the PDF if the viewer is unavailable.
entry.summary: What 22.1 million FEMA disaster assistance applications reveal about housing tenure, missing documentation, and who controls the proof.

entry.title: How National Nuclear Energy Plans Frame Small Modular Reactors

link.title: How National Nuclear Energy Plans Frame Small Modular Reactors

entry.content:
Daein Kang, John D Kim, Moe Kyaw Thu, and Brian Y An · Published in Environmental Research Letters, August 5, 2026

Small modular reactors (SMRs) have attracted interest as a potential source of reliable, low-carbon electricity, with applications that could extend beyond power generation to district heating, industrial energy services, and local grid resilience. But how are governments actually discussing SMRs in their national energy strategies—as new reactor technologies, or as part of broader urban energy transitions?

In “How national nuclear energy plans frame small modular reactors (SMRs): evidence from natural language processing of global policy documents,” we examine the policy language surrounding SMRs across 66 national and international energy plans from eight countries. We extract passages around SMR-related terms, yielding more than 800,000 words, and combine natural language processing—TF-IDF and topic modeling (LDA)—with qualitative close reading to understand which themes dominate and which receive less attention.

Study context

Our analysis begins with published energy plans and policy statements issued by national ministries and relevant agencies in the United States, Russia, France, Japan, China, the United Kingdom, South Korea, and Canada. The selected documents cover 2016–2025 and include both English-language documents and translated material. We apply NLP to extracted SMR-relevant text rather than treating all words in a national energy plan as SMR discourse.

Main findings

  • National SMR policy discourse is primarily technical. Across countries, the most prominent terms emphasize reactor design, development, technology, projects, fuel, and safety. Both TF-IDF and topic modeling reveal this emphasis.
  • Urban and socioeconomic applications receive less attention. Themes such as urban–rural equity, energy portfolio diversification, cogeneration, and climate resilience appear less prominently in the SMR-related policy text than the technical and regulatory vocabulary.
  • Less frequent does not mean absent. Qualitative close reading reveals references to low-carbon goals, community benefits, hybrid energy systems, and local economic opportunities—notably in Canadian, British, and Japanese policy documents, even when these themes are less visible in keyword rankings.
  • However, the findings concern policy framing, not actual deployment. Word-frequency rankings identify lexical prominence, not the significance of particular commitments or the reasons governments emphasize specific technologies.

The way governments frame an emerging technology affects which questions receive attention. A national conversation focused primarily on reactor design and regulatory readiness may leave less room for the broader role of SMRs in urban energy systems, including resilience, community participation, equitable benefit-sharing, and integration with other energy sources. Our findings highlight these gaps in the policy discourse of SMRs with regards to energy transition.

Kang, D., Kim, J. D., Thu, M. K., & An, B. Y. (2026). How national nuclear energy plans frame small modular reactors (SMRs): Evidence from natural language processing of global policy documents. Environmental Research Letters, 21, 154027.
entry.summary: What 66 national energy policy documents reveal about the technical focus of national small modular reactor strategies and their limited discussion of broader urban energy needs.
